analysis.one_liner: Taxes large profitable companies that buy back their own stock unless they pay workers an equal cash dividend.
analysis.headline: The Worker Dividend Act of 2019 never left the Senate Finance Committee: it was referred there the day it was introduced, September 19, 2019, and received no further action before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new tax on publicly traded companies with more than $250 million in U.S. earnings that buy back their own stock during the year but do not pay their U.S. employees a 'worker dividend.' That dividend must be at least the smaller of the buyback amount or half of earnings above $250 million, split equally among all U.S. employees on top of normal pay. Companies that skipped it would owe a tax equal to the amount they owed their workers. The bill was introduced by Senator Booker with one cosponsor and was referred to the Finance Committee, where it sat until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. employees — including part-time workers, pro-rated by hours — of big, profitable publicly traded companies that repurchase their own stock. Every covered employee would receive the same payment, on top of regular compensation, within 60 days of year-end unless the employer elects to fold it into a documented, permanent raise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees of large profitable public companies

how_it_helps.text: A covered employer must pay each U.S. employee an equal 'worker dividend' of at least the lesser of the amount it spent buying back its own stock, or 50% of U.S. earnings above $250 million (EBITDA), paid in addition to ordinary compensation.
Part-time employees receive a pro-rated amount based on hours worked, so low-wage and part-time workers are covered, not just salaried staff.

A company that fails to pay the dividend owes a tax equal to the required dividend, and must report its buybacks and dividend payments to the Treasury and the SEC, with rules to prevent companies from disguising the dividend as ordinary pay.

analysis.who_pays: The companies and their shareholders. A covered company either redirects buyback money into an equal cash bonus for its workforce or pays an equivalent tax; either way, money that would have gone to repurchasing shares stops flowing to shareholders.

drawbacks.text: A company can avoid the tax entirely by simply not buying back its own stock, which would leave workers with nothing while shareholders lose the buyback — the bill gives firms an easy exit that could shrink total shareholder returns without raising any wages.

Because the dividend must be split equally across the entire U.S. workforce, at companies with hundreds of thousands of employees the per-worker payment could be small even when buybacks are in the billions, limiting the benefit to any individual worker.
The tax applies only to companies with U.S. earnings above $250 million, so many large public companies with thinner U.S. profits could continue buybacks with no worker payment at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's upside is real but conditional: it targets a narrow group — large, highly profitable public companies that spend heavily on buybacks — and forces a share of that money to hourly and salaried workers alike. Its main weaknesses are that companies can escape by simply cutting buybacks (good for shareholders' discipline, useless for wages), that equal distribution dilutes per-worker amounts at giant firms, and that only companies above the earnings threshold are touched. It is a focused nudge, not a broad wage policy, and it never received a hearing or a vote to test either the design or the support.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died there.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the bill on September 19, 2019, with Senator Casey as its only cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Finance.
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in the bill's action history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
With only two sponsors out of 100 senators and no committee activity, the bill had effectively no path to a floor vote in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies that buy back their own stock kept those dollars flowing to shareholders without any worker-dividend requirement, because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and there was no vote or committee action, so the partisan split on the merits was never tested; the bill's sponsor list — two Democrats out of 100 senators — gives no evidence of cross-party support.

industries.note: Any covered company that buys back stock would either divert that money to an equal employee dividend or pay an equal tax. Its interest in avoiding that requirement runs against the workers the bill would pay.
Buybacks are the main channel for returning cash to shareholders; a required worker dividend paid from the same pool of money would reduce or displace repurchases.

industries.industry: Corporate executives whose pay is tied to stock price
industries.note: Executive compensation often rides on share price, and buybacks raise share prices by shrinking share count; a tax or worker dividend on buybacks presses directly on that mechanism.
